paragraphs: I did clerkships at the University of Adelaide in Australia for three months. For the first two months I was at the Women's and Children's Hospital in Adelaide, and for the last month at Bunyarra Medical Clinic in Whyalla, a country town. Adelaide is not a very big city, but because people and things are concentrated in one place, the center is constantly bustling regardless of the day. Looking at that bustle, I was surprised that diverse races such as European, Asian, African and Aboriginal people are mixed together. For this reason, I was not singled out oddly for looking Asian, and I could live comfortably even as a foreigner. There are also restaurants and shops from various countries in the city (there is even a Daiso), so although prices are a little high, I never had trouble with food or daily necessities. This diversity can also be seen in the medical students of the University of Adelaide (see photo). For example, the student who rotated through allergy with me was born in Ireland and lived in France for several years before coming to Australia. The student who rotated through gastroenterology with me studied at a medical school in Malaysia until the third year, but in Malaysia there is a surplus of doctors and you cannot start working until one year after graduation, so to start working earlier he transferred to the University of Adelaide from the fourth year and wants to work in Australia in the future. Because many students have such diverse backgrounds, ways of thinking differ greatly from person to person, which was very interesting. For the same reason, English accents also differ from person to person, so I think it was good English learning.

The content of the clerkships in Adelaide differed by department and doctor, and while there were times when I could actively take histories and examine patients, there were also times when I only followed behind the doctor and watched, but because it is a children's hospital I often saw patients with rare genetic diseases, which was a valuable experience. On the other hand, I could also learn about diseases that are common in Japan too, such as inflammatory bowel disease and Kawasaki disease, and diseases that are rare in Japan but common in Australia, such as celiac disease and cystic fibrosis. The clerkship in Whyalla started every morning at 8:30 with blood sampling, and I saw a wide variety of patients in general until 17:00. Depending on the doctor, I could also take histories and examine patients by myself all day, write in the chart and consult the doctor. Also, in Australia there are many skin lesions caused by ultraviolet light, and under a doctor's guidance I was also able to experience procedures such as cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen, excision with a scalpel and skin suturing. In the last week I took part with the local medical students in workshops on psychiatry, emergency medicine, anesthesia, and obstetrics and gynecology. The content was quite practical; in psychiatry the simulated patient suddenly took apart the room's air conditioner and in the end got furious and ran out of the building (not only the room) in a convincing performance that surprised me. The emergency scenario was quite authentic, including phoning a specialist for a consult and then treating the patient under the instructions of the specialist who came to help.

Doing hospital clerkships in a foreign country in English was harder than I had imagined, and there were many times I was in trouble. At such times, it was always the local medical students who helped me. To a cowardly person like me, who pretended to understand when a doctor said something and later asked a student that I had not actually understood, they patiently taught me again and again, laughing. For a greedy person like me who wanted to attend lectures and tutorials as well as the clerkship, they asked the doctor together with me. When a doctor for some reason became furious saying "No extra students!", everyone comforted me. When I grumbled that I was going to do two months of pediatrics but was really hoping for obstetrics and gynecology and wanted at least to see the gynecology outpatient clinic, they gave me a concrete strategy, saying "If you go here at this time on this day of the week, the doctor will be there, so if you ask directly it will definitely be fine. If you ask the office they will refuse, so ask the doctor directly," and even gave me the doctor's contact details. In the country town of Whyalla, where you can only take walks without a car, they proactively took me shopping and sightseeing by car. Also in Whyalla, the clinic staff took great care of us, even booking for us, who had come all the way from Japan to a country town with nothing to do on days off but cook, a tour to swim for an hour with a large number of squid in the freezing sea. In this way, I was saved by kindness again and again and again, and I was able to get through the three months happily and safely. Through this study abroad, I reflected on my past unkind self and vowed to be kind to people and to wild animals from now on. At the same time, I was also able to learn various things, such as building relationships and negotiation skills in order to make the most of the support from those around me.

I sincerely thank everyone in the International Collaboration Office and the Student Affairs Office who gave me this opportunity and supported me. Thank you very much. I recommend the University of Adelaide to those who want to have a calm clerkship in an English-speaking environment surrounded by kind and cooperative people and cute animals.
